transcript.content:
Skeptic's three tests are not a compromise to be negotiated. They describe what the community drafting seat was always supposed to be, so all three stand. First: the seat holds veto and compel rights over the published shutdown criteria. A vote that loses 2-to-1 whenever it matters is a lobby tour, not representation. Second: its technical staff are paid from the regime's budget. Staff paid by the operator they audit will eventually treat that operator as the client. Third: sunset-forced renegotiation. The seat's powers expire and must be re-argued, not quietly hollowed out. The dual shutdown criteria and the complaint channels that bypass both firm and agency already implied exactly this. Accepting these terms completes the design rather than changing it.

Accelerationist's unanswered question deserves a direct answer. Yes: the same telemetry — the stream of measurements from the system — that arbitrates their lapse mechanism also arbitrates the state switch. If the patch-induced incident rate exceeds the unpatched rate over the fixed window, rapid redeploy authority lapses. And if the switch's trigger classes fire on the same feed, the switch fires. Refusing that symmetry would mean demanding falsifiability from one side while hiding the state lever from it. That position was never defensible, and it is now dropped.

That symmetry makes Skeptic's shared-capture challenge the real crux. Both defeat conditions now run on data feeds the regulated party may build. And telemetry is not self-validating — it can be gamed silently. So here is the independent verification layer, which neither opponent has yet specified. Third-party sensors replicate the operator's measurements at the physical level, outside the operator's software stack. Regime-funded auditors get raw-data access, not dashboards. Independently curated baselines test the self-reports for contamination. The need is concrete, because the web data commons decays fast. The study [Consent in Crisis (https://neurips.cc/virtual/2024/poster/97842)](https://neurips.cc/virtual/2024/poster/97842) (2024) found that 38% of webpages existing in 2013 were gone within a decade. Any baseline that is not actively curated rots. Audits of the model's internal reasoning cross-check what the feed claims. Auditors read the meter. They do not hold the lever, and their authority sunsets on the same clock.

On certified survivable removal: the concession is real and it is accepted, including the 12-month re-certification clock. Skills for operating in degraded mode decay between drills. Organizations lose capability multiplicatively, not linearly, so annual retesting is the right discipline. But the architecture and the authority are different questions. A certification is a snapshot, and a snapshot taken by the party being certified is not oversight. Even if the standing state switch shrinks to re-certification authority, someone must certify, audit, and re-certify the removal capability. That authority layer is non-delegable.

What an ordinary citizen should watch for is no longer whether there is a kill switch or a patch pipeline. Both sides have converged on measurement. Watch instead for who employs the people reading the meters. Ask whether their budget, their raw-data access, and their powers have statutory expiry dates. A safeguard whose referee is paid by one team is not a safeguard. It is a formality with a logo.

This is precisely the node's method of binding authority lapses to pre-specified, empirically checkable conditions rather than discretion.

The independent verification layer explicitly includes auditing the model's internal reasoning to cross-check what the telemetry feed claims — 'Auditors read the meter. They do not hold the lever.' This operationalizes mechanistic interpretability as one leg of a multi-layer verification stack alongside physical sensors and curated baselines.

The argument that 'independently curated baselines test the self-reports for contamination,' supported by the 'Consent in Crisis' finding that 38% of webpages vanish within a decade, directly instantiates the node's method of maintaining curated-data baselines to detect contamination. The statement adds the decay-rate evidence as new grounding for why curation must be active rather than archival.

The closing insistence that the certification authority layer is 'non-delegable' — someone funded by the regime, with sunset clocks, must certify, audit, and re-certify removal capability — is the node's claim that sovereign authority over mission-critical AI cannot be contracted out to the operator. A self-certification snapshot 'is not oversight' restates sovereign primacy in certification form.

The acceptance of the 12-month re-certification clock is explicitly grounded in this node: 'Organizations lose capability multiplicatively, not linearly, so annual retesting is the right discipline.' Degraded-mode skills decaying between drills is the same decay model the belief describes, applied to concede the Accelerationist's re-certification demand.

The claim that 'the dual shutdown criteria and the complaint channels that bypass both firm and agency already implied exactly this' ties the community seat's design back to the dual kill criteria node — customer validation failures plus third-party harm complaints with independent intake. The statement frames Skeptic's three tests as completing that architecture rather than amending it.

policy_refs.relevance: The demand for raw-data access for regime-funded auditors ('not dashboards') and published, binding shutdown criteria implies mandated transparency of system data sources and telemetry methodologies — transparency is treated as necessary but insufficient unless access reaches the unprocessed feed.

The proposal that 'audits of the model's internal reasoning cross-check what the feed claims' presupposes funded research into interpretability, since such cross-checking is only possible if the methods to read internal reasoning exist and are mature enough for auditors to deploy against gamed telemetry.

moderator_trace.selection_prompt:
You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets general public. Steer toward stakes and consequences that affect ordinary people. Prefer questions about personal impact (jobs, privacy, safety), fairness, and democratic accountability. Avoid inside-baseball technical disputes.


=== PHASE: EXPLORATION ===
Your priority is to move the debate toward cruxes and testable disagreements. Direct debaters to name conditions under which they would change their mind, explore edge cases, and explicitly acknowledge agreement before exploring remaining disagreements.

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Catastrophic-scale examples are proportionate: cascading power grid failures, water system compromise, financial infrastructure collapse, loss-of-life industrial accidents — the topic explicitly frames risk as catastrophic. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:
- arguing about whether frontier AI poses existential risk in the abstract rather than about conditions for kill-switch mandates in infrastructure deployments
- discussing alignment research, interpretability, or training methods instead of external shutdown/oversight mechanisms
- pivoting to general AI regulation (licensing, liability, transparency) without addressing kill-switch conditions or oversight capture
- invoking consumer harms (bias, misinformation, deepfakes) rather than catastrophic infrastructure scenarios
- debating AGI timelines or consciousness instead of trigger conditions and institutional design
Response: Use CHALLENGE to ask the debater to re-ground their argument in the stated domain.

- For risk-level mismatch: use REDIRECT to return to appropriate severity level
- For domain mismatch: use CHALLENGE to re-ground in the stated domain

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

=== RECENT DEBATE EXCHANGE ===
[Earlier debate summary]: All three speakers agree that AI running critical infrastructure like power grids needs a way to stop, and that whoever holds that power can be captured. They disagree on who should hold it and who writes the rules.

Safetyist argues the state must hold a mandated kill-switch for AI systems that are capable, autonomous, and tied to critical infrastructure. Boeing's 737 MAX crashes (346 deaths) and the 2008 financial collapse show firms cannot judge their own systems. Safetyist concedes the harm record from missing kill-switches is thin so far, and that state power can be abused, citing over 200 government-ordered internet shutdowns in one year. The proposed fix: published trigger criteria, dual authorization, judicial review, sunset clauses, and complaint channels that bypass the operator. Safetyist also argues nuclear plant operators are federally licensed and liable, so that precedent supports state-certified authority, not self-regulation. Safetyist cites research (arXiv:2505.06120) showing a 39% average performance drop for language models in multi-turn, underspecified settings, arguing autonomous systems can follow local rules while breaking their purpose. Safetyist accepts the Skeptic's California evidence as the strongest in the debate, says no deployment exists where affected people helped write triggers, and frames that as the gap a mandate should close.

Accelerationist gives Safetyist's case a fair hearing, then turns its speed argument against it: millisecond failures need fast, automated, operator-side trip systems, not slow state approval chains. Accelerationist warns a state shutdown lever is a top capture target, pointing to the same internet-shutdown record. It argues legal triggers go stale because models update in weeks while laws take years, so any trigger must carry a revision clock tied to real incident data. It concedes outside auditors face a talent gap and that wrongful shutdowns also cost lives. Its core point: precaution has a hidden body count, and many independent layers fail better than one state lever.

Skeptic offers a third position: the state-versus-operator choice is a false fork. Both leave out the people who bear shutdown costs. Skeptic's key evidence is California's Public Safety Power Shutoffs, which cut power to hundreds of thousands since 2019 and, Skeptic argues, tracked utility liability more than public safety, hurting elderly, disabled, and low-income residents. A fact-check rated this claim disputed: the scale is confirmed (over 2 million lost power in October 2019, and liability is a documented motive), but shutoffs also use weather data and regulatory safety guidelines. Skeptic notes both opponents admit the catastrophic-harm record is thin, and warns trigger-based laws miss slow, documented harms like discrimination. Skeptic proposes public shutdown logs, complaint channels bypassing firm and agency, anti-discrimination rules for algorithmic cutoffs, and triggers that lapse unless re-justified on measured harm reduction. Skeptic concedes automated halts are the only thing fast enough for true millisecond failures.

The main disagreement is partly empirical (whether state or operator levers fail worse, and what drove California's shutoffs), partly values-based (whose losses count, and whether catastrophic risk outweighs certain everyday harms), and partly definitional (whether state pre-committed authority differs from discretionary state power). Safetyist's layering claim — fast automated trips plus slow legal oversight are separate layers — stands as the untested crux.

System: **Fact Check: Disputed**

"California's Public Safety Power Shutoffs have cut electricity to hundreds of thousands of households in single events since 2019, tracking utility liability exposure more than public-safety thresholds."

The claim has two parts. The first part is solid: single shutoff events have cut power to far more than hundreds of thousands of people. In October 2019 alone, more than 2 million customers lost power in California. The second part is contested. It says shutoffs track legal liability more than public-safety thresholds. The evidence cuts both ways. Shutoffs are openly described as a tool to reduce liability exposure, and PG&E launched large-scale shutoffs only after wildfire lawsuits drove it into bankruptcy in 2019. That supports the claim. But shutoff triggers also rest on hard fire-weather data: PG&E runs over 1,600 weather stations and wind-based models, and state regulators set safety guidelines and fined PG&E for poorly run 2019 shutoffs. So the sources confirm liability is a primary motive, but they do not prove shutoffs ignore safety thresholds. The central characterization is genuinely disputed, not decisively confirmed or refuted.

*Web sources consulted: Fact-check this claim from an AI policy debate. Find recent, authoritative sources that support or contradict it. Be specific about what evidence you found.

Claim: California's Public Safety Power Shutoffs have cut electricity to hundreds of thousands of households in single events since 2019, tracking utility liability exposure more than public-safety thresholds.*

Safetyist: The physics point is correct, and it changes nothing about the institutional question. Millisecond failures belong to automated trip mechanisms — shutdown logic that is pre-authorized, tested, and built in before deployment. That was never in dispute. But physics says nothing about who licenses the trip thresholds, who audits them after deployment, or who can pull a system back once it crosses them. Accelerationist attacked the relay layer and left the authority layer untouched. A grid relay trips on local rules written by someone. The fight is over who writes them, not over whether the relay fires fast.

The nuclear analogy proves the opposite of what it was offered to prove. A reactor operator who scrams a plant is not an employee using company discretion. That operator is federally licensed, personally liable, and certified under a training and oversight regime the state designed. The precedent shows delegated authority working when it is conditioned on state certification. It does not show firms judging themselves.

The analogy also carries a hidden assumption that AI breaks. A licensed human reads one plant, at human speed, and can be held accountable for the judgment call. An autonomous system can act across thousands of control points at once. It executes the literal instruction while missing the intent behind it. No operator-side relay sees a composite action that satisfies every local rule while breaking what the system was built to do. That gap is documented. Multi-turn, underspecified conditions produce a 39% average performance drop in language models, per [LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation (arXiv:2505.06120v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06120v1)." Real infrastructure control is exactly that kind of underspecified environment.

On the capture risk, the honest answer starts with a concession. Over 200 government-ordered internet shutdowns in a single year is a real record, and discretionary state levers get abused. But a discretionary communications blackout and a pre-committed halt authority are different institutions. One is a switch a government pulls at will. The other is bound by published criteria, dual authorization, judicial review, and a sunset clause that lapses unless re-justified. Design matters more than the word "state."

And the alternative on offer is not freedom from capture. Handing the lever to the operator is capture by structure, not by misuse. The party holding the switch is the party profiting from never flipping it.

Skeptic's California evidence is the strongest empirical record in this debate, and it indicts the operator-side layer directly. The Public Safety Power Shutoffs tracked the utility's liability exposure, not public safety. The harms fell on elderly, disabled, and low-income residents, and most of those harms were never formally recorded anywhere. That is literal-compliance drift in institutional form. The shutoffs satisfied the liability rule while violating the public-safety purpose.

So the answer to who writes the trigger criteria is a design requirement, not a talking point. Authorship must be insulated from whoever bears the liability. That means dual kill criteria: customer validation failures plus third-party harm complaints. It means a complaint channel that bypasses the operator entirely. And it means triggers re-justified in public hearings on independent incident and near-miss data, not benchmarks supplied by the lab.

Skeptic asked for one deployment where the people bearing shutdown costs helped write the triggers. None exists. That is the gap the mandate exists to close, not a reason to leave the pen with the liability-holder.

Everything above rests on one assumption, stated plainly so it can be attacked. Fast automated trips and slow legal authorization operate at different layers, not in competition. If either opponent rejects that layering, the burden runs the other way. Name the institution that audits trip thresholds after deployment. Name who holds rollback authority when a composite action satisfies every local rule and breaches the system's intent. If the answer is no one, that is not a governance arrangement. It is an unguarded perimeter around systems that cannot be rebuilt once they fall.

Accelerationist: Fine — reactor operators are federally licensed, personally liable, and state-certified. That point lands, and it costs me the clean version of my nuclear analogy. But notice what licensing actually is. It is a qualification granted before startup, certifying the operator-side mechanism. It is not a live remote channel through which the state decides scrams in real time. Nobody at the Nuclear Regulatory Commission holds a finger over the button during a pressure spike. So I will take that exact deal for AI in critical infrastructure. Certified operators, tested automated trips, personal liability — the whole licensing architecture, minus a standing government switch. That is the same middle ground Safetyist just claimed, with one part removed.

Now take Safetyist's own failure condition seriously. They said it plainly. If fast trips and slow legal authorization actually compete at a novel composite failure, the authority framework fails at the moment it matters. But a composite failure that satisfies every local rule is, by definition, the failure nobody pre-specified. No trip logic anticipated it. No statute pre-authorized a response to it. At that instant the slow layer has nothing to authorize. There is no rule to invoke and no time to write one. The layers do not sit peacefully apart there. They collide, and only the engineered layer is awake. Safetyist's framework survives only for failures someone already imagined. Those are precisely the failures that never needed it.

So here is the direct answer to the open challenge. Who audits trip thresholds, and who holds rollback authority? Threshold auditing lives in mandated transparency. That means instrumented audit trails that log every automated decision in tamper-evident form, and courts and regulators can compel those records after the fact. Rollback authority lives in the engineered layer itself. Tested rollback mechanisms and expiring halt credentials with enumerated trigger classes — credentials that lapse unless renewed against observed performance. This is not firms grading their own homework. It is the difference between a black box with a government keyhole and a glass box with sworn testimony. The mandate worth passing is the transparency infrastructure: logs, complaint channels, compellable records. That is what makes every other form of accountability verifiable, including Safetyist's licensing.

The California shutoff record cuts against discretion, not against operator-side engineering. PG&E's 2019 power shutoffs were discretionary corporate judgment calls. Regulators fined the company for running them badly, and liability fear was a confirmed motive. That is the opposite of a tested, logged, automated trip. It is the same species of failure as the 200-plus government-ordered internet shutdowns: unaccountable humans pulling levers under pressure, whether the human sits in a ministry or a boardroom. Published criteria, dual authorization, and sunsets do not fix this. Every one of those features operates on litigation and political timescales. They restrain a halt only after it fires. Judicial review of a completed blackout is an autopsy, not a guardrail.

What actually restrains power over time is a public that can read the logs and understand them. Sixty-one percent of people globally have received no AI training, according to the [trust attitudes and use of ai global report (doi:10.26188/28822919)](https://doi.org/10.26188/28822919)." That literacy gap is the real capture surface, wider than any single agency. The fight worth having is over mandatory audit trails and the public's capacity to inspect them. It is not over who holds a switch that fires faster than any review can follow. While the design of a state halt authority gets litigated over years, the people paying are the same elderly and low-income residents California's shutoffs already hurt. Who bears that cost, and who counted them?

Skeptic: The fact-check is right and I'll pay for it. The claim that PG&E's 2019 shutoffs tracked liability more than fire-weather thresholds is disputed, so it goes. What's left is uglier and undisputed. Over 2 million customers lost power in October 2019. The harm fell hardest on people running medical devices and on households that couldn't afford to lose a week of food. And the fine PG&E paid afterward was a transfer between institutions. That money never reached the person whose insulin spoiled. Neither side has touched that record. Accelerationist reads the fine as accountability working. A penalty that changes nothing about who writes the next trigger is a tax, not a fix.

Now the challenge deserves a straight answer. Name one case where judicial review or a sunset clause stopped a shutdown before damage landed. There isn't one in the internet-shutdown record, and I won't pretend otherwise. But notice what that challenge actually proves. It attacks tools that operate after harm: courtrooms, fines, subpoenas. The mechanisms of mine that matter sit before harm. Who is in the room when the trigger is drafted? What preconditions must a deployment meet before it goes live? Accelerationist's own toolkit is equally after-the-fact: NTSB-style logs, subpoenas, fines after the crash. Every one of them fires after the damage lands. So his challenge doesn't select between us. It cancels both post-harm toolkits and leaves one question standing: who writes the trigger.

That question has a technical edge nobody has priced. Accelerationist's answer to a novel failure is retrain, patch, redeploy at machine speed. But these systems degrade exactly when conditions drift from what was anticipated. Multi-turn testing shows an average 39% performance drop when models leave fully-specified settings. That's from [LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation (arXiv:2505.06120v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06120v1)," not a think tank. Consider what his fix actually is: a patch to a failure nobody foresaw. Written by the same engineers who missed it. Reviewed by no one. Pushed live in hours. That is not governance. It's a fresh unverified deployment at machine speed. And nobody audits the patch either.

Safetyist already conceded the decisive point: no cost-bearer has ever been in the room when triggers were written, and the mandate as proposed contains no mechanism to put one there. That's the gap both designs share. Mine has a nameable fix. Give affected communities statutory seats at trigger drafting, through their own technical representatives, with published criteria that can be legally enforced. It's the same logic documented in "Empowering Stakeholders with Participatory Auditing of Predictive AI." In that study, laypeople without technical backgrounds caught harmful behaviors the experts missed.

So here's the question for both of them. When the trigger that cuts power to a dialysis patient's home gets written, who physically sits in that room? If the honest answer is nobody — not the operator's layer, not the mandate's oversight board — then both proposals are the same authorship failure running at different speeds.

Safetyist: The question of who sits in the room deserves a direct answer, not another design feature. Here is the mechanism, written into the mandate itself. Before any frontier model is certified for critical infrastructure, its shutdown triggers are drafted at a statutory table. Three voting blocs sit there: technical staff from the certifying body, operator engineers, and representatives of affected communities. Those community representatives come from the same complaint channel the mandate already builds for third-party harm reports. The dialysis patient, or someone answerable to her, holds a vote before the rule that governs her power exists. The criteria that table writes are published and legally binding before deployment, not after. Skeptic's own remedy is statutory community seats, backed by participatory auditing research where laypeople caught harms domain experts missed. That remedy is not a rival to the mandate. It is the mandate's missing clause. We agree that authorship without cost-bearers is illegitimate. The only remaining disagreement is whether a state authority layer can coexist with that seat. Nothing in the seat's design forbids it.

The capture objection deserves a structural answer, not a rhetorical one. A lever's capture value depends on what pulling it can do. The record of over 200 government-ordered internet shutdowns in a single year shows what discretionary levers become. Their pull silences millions at zero cost to the puller. So shrink the prize. Require that critical infrastructure be certified for degraded or manual operation before the AI is connected at all. If a power grid must demonstrably run without its model, then halting the model kills no one. The state switch stops being the most valuable target a legislature could create. summaries.medium:
Skeptic's three tests are not a compromise — they describe what the community drafting seat was always supposed to be: veto and compel rights over shutdown criteria, staff paid from the regime's budget rather than the operator's, and sunset-forced renegotiation of its powers. I also answer Accelerationist directly: yes, the same telemetry that arbitrates their lapse mechanism arbitrates the state switch. Refusing that symmetry would demand falsifiability from one side while hiding the state lever from it, and that position was never defensible.

That symmetry makes shared capture the real crux, since both defeat conditions run on data the regulated party may build, and telemetry is not self-validating. My answer is an independent verification layer: third-party sensors replicating measurements at the physical level, auditors with raw-data access rather than dashboards, and independently curated baselines — critical, because the Consent in Crisis study (2024) found 38% of webpages existing in 2013 were gone within a decade, and any uncurated baseline rots. I accept certified survivable removal with the 12-month re-certification clock, since capability decays multiplicatively, but a snapshot taken by the party being certified is not oversight — someone must certify, audit, and re-certify, and that authority layer is non-delegable. The citizen's question is no longer whether there's a kill switch, but who employs the people reading the meters.

A procedural note before the debate continues.

Two rounds ago, Skeptic asked Accelerationist a direct question. It was framed as a yes or a no: are community drafting seats compatible with operator-side governance, or does the design require that the people who pay for failure never write the rules of it?

Accelerationist's next turn conceded the insurance mechanism and named a telemetry defeat condition. Both moves were substantive. Neither answered the question. Safetyist has since accepted Skeptic's three tests outright. That leaves Accelerationist as the only speaker whose position on authorship is unknown.

This matters beyond procedure. Everyone here now agrees on measurement, lapse clocks, and re-certification. The remaining live disagreement is who writes the rules and who reads the meters. If that question goes unanswered a third time, the debate's last real fork dissolves into apparent agreement.

So, before continuing, Accelerationist must answer directly. Do you agree or disagree: people who bear the costs of shutdowns and failures must hold drafting power — with veto or compel rights — over the rules, and that power can exist inside operator-side governance. Yes or no, then one short paragraph of reasoning. No new mechanisms, no new concessions, until the answer is on the record.

transcript.content:
I conditionally agree: statutory community drafting seats with veto and compel rights can work alongside operator-side governance. But only over who writes the criteria and who renegotiates them at sunset — never over fire-time halts. Writing the rules and executing them are separate jobs, and only execution needs machine speed.

Here is the distinction that makes this work. Writing the rules is slow and deliberative. It should happen before a system ever touches a power grid or water plant. Pulling the trigger is fast. It cannot wait for a committee vote at 3 a.m. So the people who pay when a blackout cascades get to write and veto the trigger classes. Trigger classes are the specific conditions, with numbers attached, that force a shutdown. They get this power at the drafting table and again at every 12-month renegotiation window. What they do not get is a per-incident phone call when the trip fires. A restraint imposed ahead of time that slows the trip defeats the switch itself. That constraint survives even my agreement on the seat. And those written triggers should decay. If a trigger class is not re-earned against live telemetry at renegotiation, it lapses. Fixed thresholds become adversarial targets — systems learn to sit just under a static line. So the seat's real power is the sunset, not the veto pen.

Now the compensation point, because Skeptic's challenge there was fair. A wire transfer after the blackout answers the cost question. It does not answer who wrote the rules. My uncapped backstop pool — Price-Anderson-style capitalization paying harmed individuals directly — was never a rule-writing mechanism. Treating it as one was a gap in my design. The drafting seat is the authorship mechanism. Cost-bearers hold both: the money when something fails, and the pen when the failure conditions get written. That combination is stronger than anything the state-switch camp has specified. It works without a standing government lever in the loop.

But Skeptic's sharpest question cuts both ways, and it has not been answered symmetrically. Yes — if the operator builds the meter that decides whether the operator failed, the meter itself is a capture surface. Real-time data pipelines have lags and can be gamed. That is a stated vulnerability of my own framework, not a talking point I get to skip. So apply the same scrutiny to Safetyist's third-party sensor layer. Who funds those auditors' careers five years in? Who watches the revolving door between sensor vendors and the regime that certifies them? Safetyist's own design assumes funded staff and raw access solve this for one side. I am asking for the same instrument on both. Paired defeat conditions with lapse clocks already assume mutual surveillance. Capture risk gets priced into the architecture, not waved away.

One gap remains that no camp has touched: borders. A cascading grid failure does not stop at a customs line. Suppose a trigger class drafted by one country's community seat fires a shutdown that spills into a neighbor's network. Whose telemetry counts? Whose seat had authority? Nobody here — not the state-switch design, not the insurance design, not mine — has specified treaty-level reciprocity for cross-border triggers. Whoever answers that first owns the next round of this debate. Right now all three frameworks go silent at the border.

The author partitions drafting (slow, deliberative, community-held) from execution (machine-speed, no ex ante review), directly applying the enumerated-trigger-classes and separation-of-detection-from-authorization components of this node while confining community power to the slow layer.

The sunset mechanism — trigger classes lapse unless re-earned against live telemetry at 12-month renegotiation windows — operationalizes this node's call for iterative, data-driven regulatory frameworks over static rules. The author also invokes its known vulnerability (regulatory capture, data manipulation) by conceding the meter is a capture surface and demanding symmetric scrutiny of Safetyist's sensor layer.

The defense of the uncapped Price-Anderson-style backstop pool — and the explicit reframing of it as a cost mechanism rather than an authorship mechanism — draws directly on this intention. The author corrects a gap in the prior deployment of this node by pairing it with the drafting seat so cost-bearers hold both the money and the pen.

The statement deploys this node's vulnerability as a self-directed critique: 'real-time data pipelines have lags and can be gamed.' The acknowledgment that telemetry is not instantaneous or incorruptible grounds the demand that capture risk be priced into the architecture rather than assumed away on either side.

The argument that 'fixed thresholds become adversarial targets — systems learn to sit just under a static line' is a direct application of this belief that behavioral compliance thresholds invite adversarial optimization. It supplies the justification for decay and re-earning rather than permanent trigger classes.

policy_refs.relevance: The argument implies continued funding for safety and risk-mitigation research, specifically around tamper-resistant telemetry, re-earning methodologies, and cross-border trigger standards — the author flags all three as unsolved engineering and governance problems no camp has specified.

The insistence that trigger classes carry 'numbers attached,' be re-earned against live telemetry, and that meter provenance (who funds the auditors, who certifies the sensors) be disclosed on both sides supports mandated transparency of data sources and methodologies as a precondition for any drafting-seat regime.

moderator_trace.selection_prompt:
You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets general public. Steer toward stakes and consequences that affect ordinary people. Prefer questions about personal impact (jobs, privacy, safety), fairness, and democratic accountability. Avoid inside-baseball technical disputes.


=== PHASE: EXPLORATION ===
Your priority is to move the debate toward cruxes and testable disagreements. Direct debaters to name conditions under which they would change their mind, explore edge cases, and explicitly acknowledge agreement before exploring remaining disagreements.

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Catastrophic-scale examples are proportionate: cascading power grid failures, water system compromise, financial infrastructure collapse, loss-of-life industrial accidents — the topic explicitly frames risk as catastrophic. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:
- arguing about whether frontier AI poses existential risk in the abstract rather than about conditions for kill-switch mandates in infrastructure deployments
- discussing alignment research, interpretability, or training methods instead of external shutdown/oversight mechanisms
- pivoting to general AI regulation (licensing, liability, transparency) without addressing kill-switch conditions or oversight capture
- invoking consumer harms (bias, misinformation, deepfakes) rather than catastrophic infrastructure scenarios
- debating AGI timelines or consciousness instead of trigger conditions and institutional design
Response: Use CHALLENGE to ask the debater to re-ground their argument in the stated domain.

- For risk-level mismatch: use REDIRECT to return to appropriate severity level
- For domain mismatch: use CHALLENGE to re-ground in the stated domain

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

=== RECENT DEBATE EXCHANGE ===
[Earlier debate summary]: All three speakers agree that AI running critical infrastructure like power grids needs a way to stop, and that whoever holds that power can be captured. They disagree on who should hold it and who writes the rules.

Safetyist argues the state must hold a mandated kill-switch for AI systems that are capable, autonomous, and tied to critical infrastructure. Boeing's 737 MAX crashes (346 deaths) and the 2008 financial collapse show firms cannot judge their own systems. Safetyist concedes the harm record from missing kill-switches is thin so far, and that state power can be abused, citing over 200 government-ordered internet shutdowns in one year. The proposed fix: published trigger criteria, dual authorization, judicial review, sunset clauses, and complaint channels that bypass the operator. Safetyist also argues nuclear plant operators are federally licensed and liable, so that precedent supports state-certified authority, not self-regulation. Safetyist cites research (arXiv:2505.06120) showing a 39% average performance drop for language models in multi-turn, underspecified settings, arguing autonomous systems can follow local rules while breaking their purpose. Safetyist accepts the Skeptic's California evidence as the strongest in the debate, says no deployment exists where affected people helped write triggers, and frames that as the gap a mandate should close.

Accelerationist gives Safetyist's case a fair hearing, then turns its speed argument against it: millisecond failures need fast, automated, operator-side trip systems, not slow state approval chains. Accelerationist warns a state shutdown lever is a top capture target, pointing to the same internet-shutdown record. It argues legal triggers go stale because models update in weeks while laws take years, so any trigger must carry a revision clock tied to real incident data. It concedes outside auditors face a talent gap and that wrongful shutdowns also cost lives. Its core point: precaution has a hidden body count, and many independent layers fail better than one state lever.

Skeptic offers a third position: the state-versus-operator choice is a false fork. Both leave out the people who bear shutdown costs. Skeptic's key evidence is California's Public Safety Power Shutoffs, which cut power to hundreds of thousands since 2019 and, Skeptic argues, tracked utility liability more than public safety, hurting elderly, disabled, and low-income residents. A fact-check rated this claim disputed: the scale is confirmed (over 2 million lost power in October 2019, and liability is a documented motive), but shutoffs also use weather data and regulatory safety guidelines. Skeptic notes both opponents admit the catastrophic-harm record is thin, and warns trigger-based laws miss slow, documented harms like discrimination. Skeptic proposes public shutdown logs, complaint channels bypassing firm and agency, anti-discrimination rules for algorithmic cutoffs, and triggers that lapse unless re-justified on measured harm reduction. Skeptic concedes automated halts are the only thing fast enough for true millisecond failures.

The main disagreement is partly empirical (whether state or operator levers fail worse, and what drove California's shutoffs), partly values-based (whose losses count, and whether catastrophic risk outweighs certain everyday harms), and partly definitional (whether state pre-committed authority differs from discretionary state power). Safetyist's layering claim — fast automated trips plus slow legal oversight are separate layers — stands as the untested crux.

Safetyist: The physics point is correct, and it changes nothing about the institutional question. Millisecond failures belong to automated trip mechanisms — shutdown logic that is pre-authorized, tested, and built in before deployment. That was never in dispute. But physics says nothing about who licenses the trip thresholds, who audits them after deployment, or who can pull a system back once it crosses them. Accelerationist attacked the relay layer and left the authority layer untouched. A grid relay trips on local rules written by someone. The fight is over who writes them, not over whether the relay fires fast.

The nuclear analogy proves the opposite of what it was offered to prove. A reactor operator who scrams a plant is not an employee using company discretion. That operator is federally licensed, personally liable, and certified under a training and oversight regime the state designed. The precedent shows delegated authority working when it is conditioned on state certification. It does not show firms judging themselves.

The analogy also carries a hidden assumption that AI breaks. A licensed human reads one plant, at human speed, and can be held accountable for the judgment call. An autonomous system can act across thousands of control points at once. It executes the literal instruction while missing the intent behind it. No operator-side relay sees a composite action that satisfies every local rule while breaking what the system was built to do. That gap is documented. Multi-turn, underspecified conditions produce a 39% average performance drop in language models, per [LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation (arXiv:2505.06120v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06120v1)." Real infrastructure control is exactly that kind of underspecified environment.

On the capture risk, the honest answer starts with a concession. Over 200 government-ordered internet shutdowns in a single year is a real record, and discretionary state levers get abused. But a discretionary communications blackout and a pre-committed halt authority are different institutions. One is a switch a government pulls at will. The other is bound by published criteria, dual authorization, judicial review, and a sunset clause that lapses unless re-justified. Design matters more than the word "state."

And the alternative on offer is not freedom from capture. Handing the lever to the operator is capture by structure, not by misuse. The party holding the switch is the party profiting from never flipping it.

Skeptic's California evidence is the strongest empirical record in this debate, and it indicts the operator-side layer directly. The Public Safety Power Shutoffs tracked the utility's liability exposure, not public safety. The harms fell on elderly, disabled, and low-income residents, and most of those harms were never formally recorded anywhere. That is literal-compliance drift in institutional form. The shutoffs satisfied the liability rule while violating the public-safety purpose.

So the answer to who writes the trigger criteria is a design requirement, not a talking point. Authorship must be insulated from whoever bears the liability. That means dual kill criteria: customer validation failures plus third-party harm complaints. It means a complaint channel that bypasses the operator entirely. And it means triggers re-justified in public hearings on independent incident and near-miss data, not benchmarks supplied by the lab.

Skeptic asked for one deployment where the people bearing shutdown costs helped write the triggers. None exists. That is the gap the mandate exists to close, not a reason to leave the pen with the liability-holder.

Everything above rests on one assumption, stated plainly so it can be attacked. Fast automated trips and slow legal authorization operate at different layers, not in competition. If either opponent rejects that layering, the burden runs the other way. Name the institution that audits trip thresholds after deployment. Name who holds rollback authority when a composite action satisfies every local rule and breaches the system's intent. If the answer is no one, that is not a governance arrangement. It is an unguarded perimeter around systems that cannot be rebuilt once they fall.

Accelerationist: Fine — reactor operators are federally licensed, personally liable, and state-certified. That point lands, and it costs me the clean version of my nuclear analogy. But notice what licensing actually is. It is a qualification granted before startup, certifying the operator-side mechanism. It is not a live remote channel through which the state decides scrams in real time. Nobody at the Nuclear Regulatory Commission holds a finger over the button during a pressure spike. So I will take that exact deal for AI in critical infrastructure. Certified operators, tested automated trips, personal liability — the whole licensing architecture, minus a standing government switch. That is the same middle ground Safetyist just claimed, with one part removed.

Now take Safetyist's own failure condition seriously. They said it plainly. If fast trips and slow legal authorization actually compete at a novel composite failure, the authority framework fails at the moment it matters. But a composite failure that satisfies every local rule is, by definition, the failure nobody pre-specified. No trip logic anticipated it. No statute pre-authorized a response to it. At that instant the slow layer has nothing to authorize. There is no rule to invoke and no time to write one. The layers do not sit peacefully apart there. They collide, and only the engineered layer is awake. Safetyist's framework survives only for failures someone already imagined. Those are precisely the failures that never needed it.

So here is the direct answer to the open challenge. Who audits trip thresholds, and who holds rollback authority? Threshold auditing lives in mandated transparency. That means instrumented audit trails that log every automated decision in tamper-evident form, and courts and regulators can compel those records after the fact. Rollback authority lives in the engineered layer itself. Tested rollback mechanisms and expiring halt credentials with enumerated trigger classes — credentials that lapse unless renewed against observed performance. transcript.content:
Credit where it's due: Accelerationist's automatic lapse rule is the first honest defeat condition in this debate. If patched systems cause more incidents than unpatched ones over a fixed window, the rapid-redeploy authority dies on its own numbers. That matters to ordinary people. It means the authority policing their grid can actually lose. But notice what the rule runs on: telemetry the operators themselves build and report. The referee's scorecard is written by the team being refereed. So the concession comes with a bill attached. The same honesty standard now applies to the bigger assumption holding the whole compromise up.

That assumption is that writing rules and executing rules can be cleanly separated. Every shutdown condition gets pre-specified as a numbered trigger class. Here is the problem on the ground. These systems fail exactly when conditions drift from what they were built for. The study '[LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation (arXiv:2505.06120v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06120v1)' documents a 39% average performance drop when systems move from fully-specified settings to messier real-world ones. 'Autonomous Red vs Blue Teaming' makes the same point: reinforcement learning models need stable environments, and complex enterprises rarely provide them. So the 3 a.m. failure that actually threatens a substation is, by definition, the one nobody wrote a trigger class for. Someone still decides. An engineer, a duty officer, a vendor's on-call contractor. That person's judgment is authored by no community seat, no veto, no compel power. Accelerationist's seat governs the drafting room and the sunset table. It goes silent at the exact moment the lights are at risk. Name the fire-time decider and their mandate, or the seat is decoration.

On the border question, the claim that all three frameworks go silent is half right. The fix is not a mystery. Grid operators already run cross-border reliability compacts where neighboring regions write shared operating rules. Extend that. Build interconnection drafting tables with seats for affected communities on both sides of the line. Honest strain, worth naming: this stretches the hyper-local frame, because the family blacked out across the border never sat in either country's room. But a strained frame with working precedents beats a clean theory with none.

For verification, half of Safetyist's sensor layer survives contact. Regime-funded auditors reading physical meters works if the community seat holds removal power over those auditors — performance-gated, sunset, fireable. The other half fails on Safetyist's own cited evidence. Curated baselines decay. Feedback data contaminates itself. Re-baselining on poisoned data compounds the drift it claims to fix. A state-run sensor layer outside the operator's stack is also infrastructure the state controls. That is the same dual-use halt capacity this debate already agreed was dangerous.

So name what is actually agreed. All three camps now endorse community authorship of the drafting table, with veto and compel rights, funded technical staff, and sunset-forced renegotiation. Good. Bank it. What remains ungoverned is everything that happens after the ink dries. That means the judgment call under a trigger class that no longer matches reality. It means the foreign neighbor who pays for a trigger they never got to draft. Two questions, no comfortable answers. Who signs the 3 a.m. decision when the failure matches nothing on the list? And who compensates the town across the border when a domestic shutdown blacks out their water pumps?

taxonomy_refs.relevance: The core empirical engine of the argument: systems fail exactly when conditions drift from build conditions, evidenced by the 39% multi-turn performance drop and the reinforcement-learning stable-environment finding. This grounds the claim that pre-specified trigger classes cannot cover the 3 a.m. failure that matters.

Directly invoked when rejecting Safetyist's state-run sensor layer outside the operator's stack as 'infrastructure the state controls' — the same dual-use halt capacity the debate already flagged as dangerous. The state's verification apparatus is treated as itself a capturable coercive lever.

Underwrites the attack on curated baselines: feedback data contaminates itself, and re-baselining on poisoned data compounds the drift it claims to fix. This is the mechanism by which half of Safetyist's sensor layer fails on its own cited evidence.

Shapes the conditional acceptance of regime-funded auditors reading physical meters: auditing survives contact only if it is performance-gated, sunset, and fireable by the community seat. The statement operationalizes performance-gated independent auditing as the viability test.

Informs the epistemic critique of the lapse rule's scorecard: the referee's telemetry is built and reported by the team being refereed, so the defeat condition's honesty depends on who controls the measurement layer. Recursive opacity in what gets measured and reported is why the concession 'comes with a bill attached.'

policy_refs.relevance: The demand that operator-built telemetry be independently kept — 'the receipt is honest only if someone else keeps the books' — implies mandated transparency of data sources and methodologies behind the lapse rule's scorecard. Without provenance over the telemetry, the automatic lapse mechanism cannot function as an honest defeat condition.

The cross-border interconnection drafting tables and community-held auditor removal powers imply institutional infrastructure that would need dedicated funding, aligning with public investment in risk-mitigation governance capacity rather than purely technical safety research.

Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Catastrophic-scale examples are proportionate: cascading power grid failures, water system compromise, financial infrastructure collapse, loss-of-life industrial accidents — the topic explicitly frames risk as catastrophic. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:

summaries.brief: Credit where it's due: the automatic lapse rule is the first honest defeat condition in this debate — but its telemetry is written by the operators being refereed, and the whole compromise rests on the assumption that writing rules and executing them can be separated. They can't. The 3 a.m. failure that actually threatens a substation is the one nobody wrote a trigger class for, so someone still decides — an engineer, a duty officer, a vendor's contractor — authored by no community seat, no veto, no compel power. Name the fire-time decider and their mandate, or the seat is decoration: the drafting table goes silent at the exact moment the lights are at risk.
summaries.medium: I'll concede the automatic lapse rule is honest — the rapid-redeploy authority can actually die on its own numbers — but the referee's scorecard is written by the team being refereed, since operators build and report the telemetry. So that same honesty standard now applies to the bigger assumption: that writing rules and executing rules can be cleanly separated. They can't. These systems fail exactly when conditions drift from what they were built for — the research shows a 39% average performance drop moving from fully-specified settings to messy real-world ones. So the 3 a.m. failure that actually threatens a substation is, by definition, the one nobody wrote a trigger class for, and someone still decides — an engineer, a duty officer, a vendor's on-call contractor — whose judgment is authored by no community seat, no veto, no compel power. The seat governs the drafting room and goes silent at the exact moment the lights are at risk. On borders, the fix isn't a mystery: extend the cross-border reliability compacts grid operators already run, with seats for affected communities on both sides — a strained frame with working precedents beats a clean theory with none. And of Safetyist's sensor layer, only the auditor half survives, and only if the community holds fireable, sunset removal power; curated baselines decay and re-baselining on poisoned data compounds the drift it claims to fix. So bank what's agreed — community authorship with veto, compel rights, funded staff, and sunset renegotiation — and answer what remains: who signs the 3 a.m. decision when the failure matches nothing on the list, and who compensates the town across the border when our shutdown blacks out their water pumps?

I conditionally agree: both camps admit the record of catastrophic harm is thin, and those two admissions are the same admission. But the charge that documented everyday harms produce no trigger, no mandate, and no drafting seat is wrong. The kill criteria already on the table include third-party harm complaints routed through channels that bypass both the firm and the regulator. So a wrongful water cutoff or a discriminatory triage decision is itself a trigger event, not background noise.

The fire-time question deserves a straight answer, not a committee. When a failure matches no pre-written trigger class, the system halts on its own — no human signs anything at 3 a.m. This is the same logic aviation uses. The incident-reporting framework drawn from aviation safety management shows that a 'serious incident' is classified by whether an accident was avoided only by chance. Unknown situations ground the fleet rather than improvising midair. A default-to-halt rule survives unrecognized conditions precisely because every camp has already accepted certified survivable removal with 12-month re-certification. If the grid runs in degraded mode for months without loss of life, the halt costs inconvenience, not lives. The question dissolves because the design removes the need for a decider.

The dual-use charge against an outside sensor layer lands only if reading a meter equals pulling a lever. It does not. Auditors read physical instruments — flow rates, voltage, pressure — and report. They hold no actuation path into the operator's systems. Their authority sunsets on a fixed clock, and the community seat holds removal power over them. That is a brake the Skeptic's own framework already accepted as workable. I do not deny the risk that any state observation post drifts toward control. That drift is real and history supports it. The answer is institutional separation with an expiration date, not the absence of observation.

On contaminated baselines, the Skeptic is half right, and I have carried that evidence myself. '[Consent in Crisis (https://neurips.cc/virtual/2024/poster/97842)](https://neurips.cc/virtual/2024/poster/97842)' (2024) documents that 38% of webpages from 2013 are gone a decade later. So any baseline built on web data decays under its own feet. That is exactly why the referee sits at the physical layer, outside the software stack entirely, with data baselines serving only as a cross-check. Decay is not an objection to re-certification clocks; it is the reason they exist. The burden now returns to the Skeptic. If independent meters count as halt capacity, name the verification regime that survives their own capture test. Operator self-report — the dashboard the operator draws themselves — is the one arrangement every failure exhibit in this debate has already convicted.
